📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that pratik Joglekar is a Senior Product Designer working with HubSpot. He loves to solve complex and challenging UX problems. When not working, he can be found at … More about Pratik ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, in 2024, an Air Canada customer asked a chatbot about bereavement fares. The bot confidently gave him a refund policy that didn’t exist. The airline refused to honor it. A tribunal ruled in the customer’s favor. The bot hadn’t decided anything; it had predicted an answer based on patterns in its training data. The company treated that prediction as policy.

It has been revealed that this is the risk at the heart of designing with AI today: probabilistic systems wrapped in deterministic interfaces. The AI offers a guess, the interface presents it as truth, and the user, or the organization, acts on it.

Recent findings suggest that humans are wired for deterministic thinking. We prefer to believe that past actions determine future outcomes. Flip a coin 999 times and get heads every time, the deterministic mind assumes the coin is rigged. The probabilistic mind accepts that the 1000th flip could still go either way. That second mindset is harder to hold onto, but it is exactly what designers need right now.

Products operate in complex, nonlinear environments, and AI is accelerating that complexity. When designers and product teams treat AI outputs as the answer rather than one of many possible answers, they build fragile experiences, and in some cases, like medical diagnostics or financial forecasting, genuinely dangerous ones.

Sources indicate that this article is a practical guide to designing probabilistically with AI as a partner. It is about using AI to sharpen your thinking rather than outsource it, accounting for model bias, human sentiment, and perceived risk along the way.

According to recent reports, most questions we ask AI do not produce binary answers. They produce probabilities based on patterns in data. If you ask, “Do aliens exist?” the answer will be somewhere between plausible and uncertain. Scientists consider life elsewhere in the universe likely, but without any concrete evidence, we cannot confirm it. The answer doesn’t resolve the question; it frames it as a probability.

Designers should read AI outputs the same way. They are signals, not conclusions, possible outcomes that have to be interpreted within the context of product goals, user behavior, and business constraints.

It has been revealed that many digital products already work this way. Netflix doesn’t know you’ll enjoy Superstore because you watched The Office; it estimates the probability and surfaces the title accordingly. The interface is responding to a prediction.

Design decisions can follow the same logic. AI models can combine behavioral analytics with research insights to estimate the likelihood of certain outcomes, and those probabilities can act as a yardstick for design strategy. Consider a scenario where analytics suggest a 60% versus 90% confidence that users will complete a purchase. At 60%, the design has to do more persuasive work, testimonials, explanations, comparisons, and reassurance signals may help the user move toward a decision. At 90%, the user is already motivated, and the design should start removing friction so the action can happen swiftly. Same screen, very different design problem.

Industry observers note that AI can also simulate outcomes using historical data and behavioral models before you commit to a direction. The value of those simulations depends heavily on how prompts are structured, the context they define, the hypothesis being tested, user motivation, and the edge cases you want stressed.

Sources indicate that I can think of one such practical use: evaluating early designs through structured prompts, especially when you don’t have direct access to the user group you’re designing for. The prompt below is a starting point for evaluating a design from the perspective of neurodivergent users as well. Treat it as a template, adapt the user group, criteria, and output format to your product, and use it as a conversation starter with your team rather than a verdict.

It has been revealed that that noted, simulations do not replace experimentation. Because models are trained on historical data, they reflect past behavior more strongly than they predict future change. Imagine designing a voice interface for elderly users who struggle with touchscreens. A model trained on mobile interaction data might predict low engagement, not because the idea lacks value, but because the dataset reflects different user behavior. Simulations should always surface assumptions, not prevent innovation.

According to recent reports, AI systems are built on historical data, more specifically, on the datasets they are trained on. That foundation shapes the outputs we receive. During the AI Summit in France, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi shared an example that illustrates this well. If you ask an AI model to generate an image of a person writing with the left hand, the output may still show a person writing with their right hand. The reason is statistical: most people are right-handed, and the training data reflects that. This may have improved over time, but the point remains relevant. I still occasionally see this behavior when generating images with similar models.

It has been revealed that what you receive is not truth. It is the most statistically likely outcome given the data available. Always ask whether past data meaningfully predicts future behavior. If additional context can improve the prediction, include it. Without context, the output is just one of many possible answers dressed up as the only one.

Recent findings suggest that confidence scores deserve the same scrutiny. Overtrusting a high-confidence output leads to the Air Canada situation. Dismissing a low-confidence one can cause teams to miss a real signal buried in noisy data. A prediction with 90% confidence is not necessarily correct, and a 40% signal is not necessarily useless. Designers must still weigh the possibilities, consider the case in front of them, and bring judgment to what the AI recommends.

Transparency is how you make that possible. As AI systems increasingly shape decisions, people need visibility into how outputs are generated, the sources, the reasoning, and the summaries behind a recommendation. Black-box systems breed distrust. Systems that reveal their reasoning let consumers evaluate outputs for themselves. That transparency is good design and ethical practice. It respects the trust people place in these tools.

Thinking in probabilities often means resisting the temptation of quick answers. AI can accelerate research and surface patterns faster than ever before, but those outputs are starting points, not final decisions.

Industry observers note that design shapes how a product is ultimately experienced — the decisions designers make determine whether the experience feels adequate, intuitive, or exceptional. And design is inherently full of assumptions and bets. Even the most rigorous research can yield multiple valid solutions to the same problem, each carrying a different probability of success.

It has been revealed that thinking probabilistically means recognizing that design decisions rarely produce binary outcomes. They lead to a range of possible results, and the role of the designer is to navigate those possibilities and identify the path most likely to create value. This mindset also builds adaptability: user needs evolve, strategies change, and sometimes ideas fail. Teams that lean on data signals, experimentation, and learning loops move faster toward the most effective solution.

Before the practical principles, one fundamental idea:.

Design decisions should be optimized for likelihood, not certainty.

It has been revealed that every design decision is a bet, not a guarantee. Even when decisions are informed by research and data, they are still based on smaller samples and assumptions about how users will behave at scale. A well-researched idea can still fail in the real world.

The Air Canada chatbot from the introduction is a design lesson as much as a legal one. The bot was doing what language models do, predicting plausible text. The interface, however, communicated that prediction with complete confidence, no caveats, no “here’s what our policy usually claims,” no obvious path to a human. The user read confidence as commitment, and legally, so did the tribunal.

Recent findings suggest that this is what happens when probabilistic systems are wrapped in deterministic interfaces. The interface transforms likelihood into certainty, and that is where the risk emerges.

Designers should avoid binary thinking — a great idea does not mean guaranteed success, and a familiar idea is not guaranteed to fail. Examine variations, confidence levels, and edge cases instead. AI can certainly help here, acting as a portfolio-thinking engine that surfaces different interpretations, highlights risks, and generates structured recommendations. The goal is not to optimize for certainty, but for value: it should always be value-driven.

Sources indicate that think of the moment in Avengers: Infinity War when Doctor Strange tells Tony Stark that out of millions of possible futures, there is only one where they win. AI cannot tell you the future, but it can help you explore the possible paths. Instead of asking whether an idea will succeed, ask AI to estimate the likelihood and get a score, and use those signals to guide decisions.

Even an actual probability is not a final answer. Imagine an AI model predicts an 80% likelihood that users prefer a minimal checkout experience. That does not mean the solution is simply “build a minimal checkout.” Data should function as a compass, not a map.

Sources indicate that these questions help designers validate predictions through usability testing and additional research. AI excels at identifying patterns, but it rarely explains why those patterns exist. Understanding motivation is still a human-centered research task.

The clearest cautionary tale here is Amazon’s experimental AI recruitment tool, which the tech giant reportedly scrapped after discovering that the model had learned to downgrade resumes from women. The training data, roughly a decade of historical hiring decisions, was skewed toward male candidates, and the model inherited that skew. It began penalizing resumes that included the word “women’s,” as in “women’s chess club captain,” and favoring language more commonly found on men’s resumes. The system was not intentionally biased — the data was. Amazon reportedly tried to adjust it and eventually shut the project down because they could not guarantee it would not surface other discriminatory patterns.

It has been revealed that examples like this are why interpreting AI output critically matters. Designers need to understand the data behind a prediction and evaluate the reliability of the models they depend on. A recommendation is only as good as the data it was trained on, and the only way to know what that data is hiding is to ask.

According to recent reports, experimentation is usually framed as a way to validate a design decision. Want to lift the click-through rate of a CTA? Run an A/B test. Probabilistic thinking reframes this. Experiments should not only confirm solutions but also reduce uncertainty.

In a recent development, traditional A/B testing is expensive. It costs engineering time, traffic allocation, and user exposure, especially when a losing variant runs against a significant chunk of your audience. AI simulations can help filter weaker ideas before they reach production by making experimentation more efficient. User needs shift constantly, and the most effective teams iterate fast.

Sources indicate that AI can help evaluate assumptions early by modeling potential outcomes based on historical and behavioral data. These simulations act as a hypothesis filter, pointing to the directions worth investing engineering effort in. This also supports personalization — different consumers may respond better to different experiences. Version A may resonate with high-intent users while version B works better for exploratory ones. Multiple experiences living side by side are not a flaw; they can be an intentional strategy.

It has been revealed that AI amplifies probabilistic thinking by surfacing scenarios, assigning likelihood scores, and enabling personalization at scale. Experimentation becomes a continuous feedback loop:.

Predict → Test → Learn → Adjust → Repeat!

Use this template to define the hypothesis:.

Sources indicate that we believe [behavioral assumption] will impact [metric] because [reason]. We’ll know we are right when [evidence].

Example: We believe simplifying the onboarding flow from 5 steps to 3 will increase completion rate because people experience decision fatigue when too many choices are presented. We’ll know we’re right when we see at least a 15% increase in step-to-step conversion with no drop in activation rate.

One of the hardest things for designers is making uncertainty understandable and actionable. When uncertainty is hidden, owners treat AI outputs as facts. When it’s communicated clearly, trust increases.

Ranges, estimates, and confidence indicators go a long way. A delivery window of “Friday to Monday” tells the truth about variability without misleading anyone, whereas a specific timestamp that slips erodes trust every time. A face recognition feature that states “this looks like Pratik, is that right?” sets more honest expectations than one that just labels the photo with a name.

Communicating uncertainty does not weaken trust — it strengthens it. The goal is not to eliminate uncertainty but to design for it intelligently.

Different consumers respond to uncertainty differently, and your design should account for that:.

AI should augment human judgment, and certainly not replace it. The most trustworthy systems are designed with clear moments where people can review, challenge, correct, or override machine suggestions. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is not a safety net — it is a refinement engine. Every override, correction, or rejection becomes high-quality feedback that improves the model over time.

Control is a prerequisite for adoption. People are more willing to rely on AI when they understand how a suggestion was generated, can evaluate its implications, and can easily intervene. Well-designed products make this explicit: who is acting, what happens if the suggestion is wrong, and where the user can step in.

According to recent reports, these interactions are also critical for system improvement. Every accept, reject, or edit is a strong signal, and compared to passive analytics, this kind of feedback produces far more meaningful training data. It closes the loop between real-world usage and model performance.

GitHub Copilot is a good everyday example. It offers inline code suggestions that developers can accept with a tab, edit, or ignore entirely. The system never commits code on the user’s behalf. Authorship stays with the humans. Every data point becomes implicit feedback about which suggestions were useful. Gmail’s Smart Compose works similarly, presenting predicted text as optional, keeping tone and intent in the user’s hands.

In higher-stakes contexts, HITL becomes more explicit. Risk and fraud systems typically use probability scores to route decisions: low-risk: proceed automatically; medium-risk: trigger additional verification; and high-risk: escalate to a human reviewer. This balances speed with judgment without removing oversight.

Sources indicate that in safety-critical domains like healthcare, human oversight is non-negotiable. AI may flag anomalies or suggest a diagnosis, but the clinician retains final authority. Tools that explain the details help the practitioner understand why a recommendation was made, reinforcing confidence without removing accountability.

From a UX perspective, HITL is about matching the interaction pattern to the level of risk. Simple accept/reject affordances work well for low-risk suggestions that improve speed without real consequences. As the stakes climb, impacting data, money, or people, preview and approval steps become essential. Explanations help people calibrate trust rather than blindly accept outputs.

What happens behind the scenes matters just as much. The system should capture user decisions with context, feed them into learning workflows, and log overrides for auditability. Over time, teams can track signals like override rate, confidence accuracy, time-to-approval, and perceived trust. A high override rate is not a user failure. It is a signal that the design or the model needs attention.

Poorly implemented HITL systems can fail in subtle ways. Human review can devolve into a rubber stamp. Workflows can slow down so much that users route around the safeguards. Feedback can skew toward a narrow subset of users. These risks are real, but they are design problems, not reasons to remove HITL.

The goal is not to maximize human involvement. It is to focus it where uncertainty, impact, or ethics demand it. Keeping HITL is less about control and more about clarity: clarity about who decides, when uncertainty matters, and how responsibility is shared between people and machines.

Good design adapts as the landscape shifts. Product design, especially in AI-powered systems, can no longer afford to optimize only for short-term conversion metrics. User intent is fluid as well as ever-changing, environments change rapidly, and probabilistic systems continuously evolve too. What works today can quietly break tomorrow. Designing for resilience means building products that stay reliable, trustworthy, and useful even as assumptions, data, and user behaviors change.

Resilient design shifts the question from:.

Sources indicate that how do we maximize this metric right now?! → How does this system behave over time, under stress, and in uncertainty?

A resilient system is one that:.

Do not just consider last quarter’s numbers. Peek into the following quarters to identify the shift and make changes accordingly.

Likelihoods shift constantly, AI models drift, contexts evolve, and user needs mature as well, so designing as if conditions are stable creates fragility in probabilistic environments. A resilient approach assumes volatility as the default.

According to recent reports, think about how recommendation systems tend to evolve. The early version of a content feed optimizes for engagement, and for a while, engagement goes up. Then customers start to notice the feed feels narrow, repetitive, maybe even exhausting. Resilient systems rebalance, introducing novelty, diversifying signals, and pulling in long-term satisfaction measures alongside short-term clicks.

Short-term conversion gains often hide long-term costs. Speeding up onboarding can reduce comprehension. Maximizing notification CTR can erode trust. Optimizing engagement alone can produce unhealthy usage patterns. Fragile systems maximize numbers while ignoring second-order effects, the downstream consequences that show up weeks or months later.

It has been revealed that duolingo’s hearts system is a good example of designing against this. It introduces friction: if you make too many mistakes, you run out of hearts and have to wait or practice older material to earn more. On paper, that looks like a conversion killer: fewer lessons per session. In practice, the team has publicly discussed how it supports long-term motivation and retention, which is the metric that actually matters for a learning app. Short-term engagement dips, but long-term outcomes improve.

Meta has made a similar, if more reluctant, shift. The organization publicly acknowledged that optimizing purely for “time spent” produced unintended emotional and societal effects, which led to a stated pivot toward “meaningful social interactions” as a guiding metric. Whether that shift fully landed is up for debate, but the acknowledgment itself is the point: optimizing for the wrong thing at scale has real downstream cost.

So, designers must routinely ask:.

Teams routinely plan for traffic spikes, but rarely for uncertainty spikes. Yet AI systems degrade, adversarial behaviors evolve, and external shocks can reshape user behavior overnight. Resilient design assumes variability and prepares for it.

Recent findings suggest that this means designing for degrading confidence. What does your interface do when the AI isn’t sure? Does it quietly fail, or does it gracefully hand off? Does the experience still make sense if AI assistance goes away entirely? A good fallback strategy is as crucial as the happy path.

If you take one thing from this article into your next design review, make it this:.

That single reframe changes how you write hypotheses, interpret AI output, scope experiments, and design for the moments when the system is wrong. Starting this week, name the assumption behind every AI recommendation you accept, find one place in your product where a probabilistic output is presented as a certainty, fix the framing, and design the fallback before the happy path.

The shift from deterministic to probabilistic design is less about upcoming tools and more about a new posture. AI has not introduced uncertainty into our world. It has simply made the uncertainty that was always there impossible to ignore. AI can estimate, simulate, and recommend, but it cannot decide what matters, which users are being overlooked, or which unconventional idea is worth defending against a model trained on yesterday’s data. Those remain human responsibilities. Think in ranges, not points. Test assumptions, not features. Build for adaptation, not perfection. In a world where prediction is cheap, and judgment is rare, the most valuable thing a designer can do is keep asking, What else might be true?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before there was Yo-Yo Ma, there was Spanish Catalan cellist and conductor Pablo Casals (December 29, 1876–October 22, 1973), regarded by many — including Yo-Yo Ma — as the greatest cellist of all time. The recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the U.N. Peace Medal for his unflinching dedication to justice and his lifelong stance against oppression and dictatorship, Casals was as much an extraordinary artist as he was an extraordinary human being — a generous and kind man of uncommon compassion and goodness of heart, a passionate spirit in love with life, and an unflinching idealist.

And yet, like many exceptional people, he cultivated his character through an early brush with suffering. In his late teenage years, already a celebrated prodigy, he underwent an anguishing spiritual crisis of the kind Tolstoy faced in his later years and came close to suicide. But with the loving support of his mother, he regained his center and went on to become a man of great talent, great accomplishment, and great vitality.

Recent findings suggest that to mark his ninetieth birthday, Casals began a collaboration with photojournalist Albert E. Kahn that would eventually become the 1970 autobiography-of-sorts Joys and Sorrows (public library) — one of the most magnificent perspectives of the creative life ever committed to words.

Straight from the opening, Casals cracks open the essence of his extraordinary character and the source of his exuberant life-energy with a beautiful case for how purposeful work is the true fountain of youth:.

On my last birthday I was ninety-three years old. That is not young, of course. In fact, it is older than ninety. But age is a relative matter. If you continue to work and to absorb the beauty in the world about you, you find that age does not necessarily mean getting old. At least, not in the ordinary sense. I feel many things more intensely than ever before, and for me life grows more fascinating.

Recounting being at once delighted and unsurprised by an article in the London Sunday Times about an orchestra in the Caucasus composed of musicians older than a hundred, he considers the spring of their vitality:.

In a recent development, in spite of their age, those musicians have not lost their zest for life. How does one explain this? I do not think the answer lies simply in their physical constitutions or in something unique about the climate in which they live. It has to do with their attitude toward life; and I believe that their ability to work is due in no small measure to the fact that they do work. Work helps prevent one from getting old. I, for one, cannot dream of retiring. Not now or ever. Retire? The word is alien and the idea inconceivable to me. I don’t believe in retirement for anyone in my type of work, not while the spirit remains. My work is my life. I cannot think of one without the other. To “retire” means to me to begin to die. The man who works and is never bored is never old. Work and interest in worthwhile things are the best remedy for age. Each day I am reborn. Each day I must begin again.

For the past eighty years I have started each day in the same manner.

With great elegance, he contrasts the dullness of mindless routine with the exhilaration of mindful ritual — something many great artists engineer into their days. In a sentiment Henry Miller would come to echo only two years later in his own memorable meditation on the secret of remaining forever young, Casals writes of his daily practice:.

It is not a mechanical routine but something essential to my daily life. I go to the piano, and I play two preludes and fugues of Bach. I cannot think of doing otherwise. It is a sort of benediction on the house. But that is not its only meaning for me. It is a rediscovery of the world of which I have the joy of being a part. It fills me with awareness of the wonder of life, with a feeling of the incredible marvel of being a human being. The music is never the same for me, never. Each day is something new, fantastic, unbelievable. That is Bach, like nature, a miracle!

Casals, indeed, finds great vitalization in bearing witness to nature’s mastery of the self-renewal so essential for the human spirit over the long run:.

In a recent development, I do not think a day passes in my life in which I fail to look with fresh amazement at the miracle of nature. It is there on every side. It can be simply a shadow on a mountainside, or a spider’s web gleaming with dew, or sunlight on the leaves of a tree. I have always especially loved the sea. Whenever possible, I have lived by the sea… It has long been a custom of mine to walk along the beach each morning before I start to work. True, my walks are shorter than they used to be, but that does not lessen the wonder of the sea. How mysterious and beautiful is the sea! how infinitely variable! It is never the same, never, not from one moment to the next, always in the process of change, always becoming something different and fresh.

In a recent development, in the same way, Casals argues, we renew ourselves through purposeful work. But he adds an admonition about the complacency of talent, echoing Jack Kerouac’s fantastic distinction between talent and genius. Casals offers aspiring artists of all stripes a word of advice on humility and hard work as the surest path to self-actualization:.

According to recent reports, I see no particular merit in the fact that I was an artist at the age of eleven. I was born with an ability, with music in me, that is all. No special credit was due me. The only credit we can claim is for the use we make of the talent we are given. That is why I urge young musicians: “Don’t be vain because you happen to have talent. You are not responsible for that; it was not of your doing. What you do with your talent is what matters. You must cherish this gift. Do not demean or waste what you have been given. Work — work constantly and nourish it.”.

According to recent reports, of course the gift to be cherished most of all is that of life itself. One’s work should be a salute to life.

Hence Ray Bradbury’s famous proclamation that he never worked a day in his life — further testament to the magic made possible by discerning your vocation.

Recent findings suggest that casals lived and worked for another four years, dying eight weeks before his ninety-seventh birthday. Joys and Sorrows remains an invigorating read — a rare glimpse into the source of this creative and spiritual vitality of unparalleled proportions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You may recognize that quiet, inner pull that comes when you least expect it, perhaps as a sense of unease that makes you change plans at the last minute, only to find out later that you narrowly missed something dangerous. Or you may feel drawn toward certain people or places without quite knowing why, only to discover later that those connections opened doors to newly introduced opportunities.

In a recent development, sometimes these signals feel obvious, like a burst of excitement in your chest or butterflies in your stomach. Other times, they show up as a quiet sense of simply knowing what to do. Whether they’re instantaneous or linger over time, they may be signs of your intuition in action.

If you don’t feel very in tune with your intuition, there’s good news: Each day, you have the opportunity to turn inward, notice your thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations, and listen to what your inner voice might be telling you. Over time, this practice of self-awareness can become a habit that helps you live more authentically and fully.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world.

Intuition stems from our nervous system, emotions, and unconscious processes working together to help us make sense of the world. Our body’s sensory networks are always at work gathering information from our environment, finding patterns from past experiences, and directing our present-day thinking and decisions.

Through our senses, our nervous system gathers information and sends signals to the brain. Regions like the amygdala help us rapidly detect potential threats, while the prefrontal cortex, which handles complex reasoning and decision-making, helps us interpret information more deliberately.

Research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

Industry observers note that that first, quick assessment happens remarkably fast. For instance, research suggests that our brains can begin detecting and interpreting subtle facial expressions in a fraction of a second.

Intuition differs from instinct, which involves automatic responses that can help protect us from danger, including reactions like fight, flight, or freeze. While instinctive responses are largely automatic, intuition draws on our past life experiences and learned patterns to help us make sense of what we encounter in daily life. Although both can feel immediate, intuitive judgments are not always accurate and may also reflect learned biases or assumptions.

Intuition can feel like a gut feeling that is hard to put into words. This is because our brain is able to look for patterns between old memories and present-day situations, using useful takeaways from the past to guide us now. This process can also include implicit, unconscious memories that we may have thought we’d forgotten.

If the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?”.

In a recent development, if the brain is key to processing intuition, then why do we often associate it with a “gut feeling?” Part of the explanation lies in the gut-brain axis, the complex communication network connecting our brain and digestive system. The walls of our digestive tract contain a network of millions of neurons that make up the enteric nervous system, or ENS.

The ENS is often called our “second brain” because it can regulate many digestive functions independently of the central nervous system. Through the gut-brain axis, digestive processes can also interact with systems involved in mood and emotion. Research has linked gastrointestinal inflammation and changes in gut function with symptoms of depression and anxiety. Most of the body’s serotonin is also produced in the digestive tract, although it doesn’t directly enter the brain. Researchers are still exploring the complex relationship between gut health and mental well-being.

This gut-brain connection helps explain why we might experience a sinking feeling in the pit of our stomach when something doesn’t feel quite right.

In a recent development, all day long, our minds are hard at work integrating rational thought with emotional intelligence (EQ). EQ helps us to become aware of and understand both our emotions and those of others. It’s a type of intelligence we can develop through emotion regulation practice, expanding our emotional vocabulary, and approaching feelings as clues to something instead of an end product.

To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively.

Sources indicate that EQ can help us manage stress, notice our assumptions, and respond more thoughtfully to difficult emotions, such as those that arise after a tense conversation. It helps us pause and remain mindful during challenging moments, and also as we choose our next steps. Developing emotional intelligence may also support our ability to recover from stressful experiences.

It has been revealed that in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), combining emotional awareness with rational thinking is known as accessing our wise mind. To be in our wise mind allows us to stay aware of feelings like fear and anger without judging them, or acting on them impulsively. Instead of automatically acting on our first reaction, we can ground ourselves while tackling emotionally painful situations.

Wisdom and living authentically are closely connected.

In a recent development, wisdom and living authentically are closely connected. As the ancient Greek maxim “Know thyself” suggests, self-knowledge is an key part of wisdom. By understanding our deeper motivations, core needs, and cherished values, we can make more intentional decisions that reflect who we are and what matters most to us.

Sources indicate that family systems therapist Virginia Satir connected personal authenticity to congruence between our internal reality and outward actions. This alignment can support our emotional well-being and help us act in ways that reflect our values. Incongruence, however, may leave us with a nagging sense that things are not quite right. Noticing incongruence in real time can help us to adjust and choose to do what feels more authentic to us and who we wish to be.

According to recent reports, sometimes, traumatic experiences can make it harder to recognize or trust our intuition, particularly when painful memories leave us feeling fearful or unsafe. Common trauma responses, such as hypervigilance to danger, will tax our nervous system, making it difficult to access the balanced perspective of our wise mind.

Trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks.

It has been revealed that trauma-based responses, such as anticipating negative outcomes in uncertain situations, can contribute to doubting our intuition and avoiding risks. Similarly, depression can affect our self-esteem and confidence, informing how we interpret upcoming situations as more negative. Holding hope for a better future might require noticing the positive patterns that run through our lives, and accessing support to process what we have gone through.

Recent findings suggest that social pressure can also make us second-guess ourselves. For example, growing up with family expectations to defer to others and put their needs first might make us believe that prioritizing our own needs is selfish. Similarly, other people’s ideas of what success looks like can make us overlook our own aspirations, such as the desire to pursue a different career path.

We may become more aware of these pressures as we get older. Hospice nurse Bronnie Ware identified five common regrets her patients shared toward the end of their lives:.

These reflections offer a reminder of the importance of making choices that align with what matters most to us.

Getting to know ourselves—our preferences, desires, and even dreams—requires making time to turn inward. A helpful practice for building the habit of self-reflecting is time in peaceful solitude. Time alone may encourage mind-wandering and daydreaming, activities associated with the brain’s default mode network, which plays a role in reflection, imagination, and our sense of self.

Quiet may even have benefits for brain health. In one study, mice exposed to periods of silence developed more immature neurons in the hippocampus, a region involved in memory and learning. Though similar effects haven’t been established in humans, the presence of young neurons in the mice is a sign of brain plasticity. And while quiet moments may sometimes feel boring, they can also create space for reflection, creativity and new ideas.

Other practices, such as spending time in nature, journaling, meditation, engaging in spiritual reflection, and limiting technology, may also strengthen our intuition and self-awareness, as we remember who we are and what we care about the most.

Clarity about our personal values is another entryway to deepening intuition. In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), values help guide meaningful action and provide direction as we navigate life’s uncertainties. They can guide our daily actions much like an inner compass would—keeping us focused on long-term goals.

Knowing our values helps us remember how we want to show up during challenging times and stay grounded when stress feels overwhelming. Values can take many forms, from nurturing relationships, to cultivating personal qualities, or finding greater joy and fulfillment in everyday life. Naming your values and writing them down may help you distinguish between choices rooted in what matters to you and those driven primarily by fear, particularly when clarity feels hard to find.

Psychotherapy can provide an intentional, supportive space where you can go inward. Therapy can also help us explore how past experiences shape our reactions, making it easier to distinguish familiar emotional patterns from what we’re noticing in the present. There are many evidence-based therapies that can help support trauma recovery, managing symptoms of anxiety and depression, and building a stronger sense of self:.

Each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves.

Thinking back to the gut feelings we began with—the caution that turned out to be right, and the inner pull that led toward newly introduced possibilities—we can see how these experiences may reflect more than coincidence. Instead, they’re signs that our nervous system, emotional intellect, mental pattern-finding, and lived experience are all working together to shape our perceptions and decisions.

Learning to trust our intuition’s guidance can take practice, particularly if difficult experiences have caused us to doubt it. But each time we pause, turn inward, and honor what we notice inside, we can build a more honest and trusting relationship with ourselves. Over time, what once felt like a faint signal may become a steady, recognizable voice that helps us move forward with greater confidence. Our capacity for intuitive wisdom is always there, and the invitation is simply to listen.

Sources indicate that marian Ting, LMFT, is a therapist and writer specializing in mood disorders, complex trauma, and AAPI mental health. She is pursuing a PhD in depth psychology at Pacifica Graduate Institute, with research interests in the synergies between self-compassion and authentic selfhood. Her writing has been published by Psychotherapy Networker, the Anxiety and Depression Association of America, and Psychedelic Support, among others. She believes beauty and struggle can coexist, and that honest self-reflection is a form of healing.

Latest Update: Kandinsky record and trove consigned by Jeff Koons buoy Christie’s 20th-century sale in New York

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in Fresh York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.
  • It has been revealed that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees).
  • It has been revealed that thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in Fresh York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

It has been revealed that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

It has been revealed that thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

It wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

The evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s Latest York in May 1986 for $1m.

Gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s Upcoming York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

In a recent development, A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s Fresh York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s Upcoming York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

Industry observers note that french painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s New York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590).

Big name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively major price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

It has been revealed that picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

According to recent reports, the Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s New York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

In a recent development, willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

One of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article stated the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

Recent findings suggest that it hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s New York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

In a recent development, though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export challenges, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

“It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” remarked Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”.

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.

The whole system starts with a single chevron. Mutabor calls it the V-Vector, a > that points forward and never sits still: it repeats into a pattern on the Appleton reception wall, frames a machine on the launch poster, and turns into punctuation inside the headlines. Voith Blue stays the signature color, and bright tones join it, a vivid royal blue for screens and a mint green for the accent word. On black, "Machines with a digital heart." puts the machine inside the chevron. On blue, "Always breaking fresh ground" lets the green >ground do the talking.

The custom typeface carries the voice. Mutabor drew it only for Voith, and it highlights in the way headlines sit: heavy, round, and set large enough that one line fills a poster. "Hydro driving renewable momentum" runs white on blue with the green >momentum as the punchline, and "Speed press" splits across a dark panel in the same weight. The VOITH wordmark stays in solid capitals, unchanged, while the type around it changes scale.

It has been revealed that one frame demonstrates the construction behind it, a lowercase a drawn with node points and thin rules beside a turbine, the letter treated like an engineered part. The grid is visible in the letterform, and the same precision runs through the system, from the wordmark lockup to the small labels on the machine diagrams.

It has been revealed that the system proves itself where the company actually works. The reception wall at Appleton carries the blue V pattern behind "Welcome to Appleton", with the VOITH wordmark set into the desk. Posters, phone screens, documents, and an agenda share the same blue, the same green, and the same chevron, from a "We are hiring" phone card to a "CSH operating principle" diagram. A purple machine close-up is labeled "nanometer precision torque drive", the product photography sitting inside the same graphic language as the posters.

Some of the case imagery is marked AI generated, Mutabor's own label on the frames, and the photography of the plants and machines reads as illustration as much as record. The rollout began in March 2026, after an internal launch in October 2025, and now runs across all markets and touchpoints. It is the first time the three business units, hydropower, papermaking, and drive technology, share one consistent, digitally native identity, and the work took the Red Dot Award for Corporate Design and Identity in 2026.

The Relief of Rock Bottom: George Orwell and the Secret Springboard of Success

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Themarginalian

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it happens to everyone — to kings and paupers, to astronauts and poets.
  • It begins with the wall — the one you hit over and over and over, not breaking through.
  • But then something extraordinary happens — something George Orwell (June 25, 1903–January 21, 1950) captures perfectly in a passage from Down and out in Paris and London (public library), recounting his experience of abject poverty while trying to become a writer, working in restaurant kitchens in Paris and wandering London as a tramp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it happens to everyone — to kings and paupers, to astronauts and poets. Nothing will protect you from it — not money, not love, not perfect health — for it spares no life that is fully lived, not the sunniest or the most privileged or the best planned.

It begins with the wall — the one you hit over and over and over, not breaking through. And then, after the exhausted collapse, the bottom. The floorboards of despair, cold as granite, absolute as gravity.

But then something extraordinary happens — something George Orwell (June 25, 1903–January 21, 1950) captures perfectly in a passage from Down and out in Paris and London (public library), recounting his experience of abject poverty while trying to become a writer, working in restaurant kitchens in Paris and wandering London as a tramp.

What Orwell observes of material poverty applies equally to the spiritual poverty of hope and meaning we call despair:.

When you are approaching poverty, you make one discovery which outweighs some of the others. You discover boredom and mean complications and the beginnings of hunger, but you also discover the great redeeming feature of poverty: the fact that it annihilates the future.

It has been revealed that it annihilates, he means, anxiety about the future, for when you have nothing left to lose, there is nothing to worry about losing. That is the relief of rock bottom — a feeling that is “a great consolation” when you are at your lowest, and one that “everyone who has been hard up has experienced”:.

It is a feeling of relief, almost of pleasure, at knowing yourself at last genuinely down and out. You have talked so often of going to the dogs — and well, here are the dogs, and you have reached them, and you can stand it. It takes off a lot of anxiety.

Two millennia before him, Marcus Aurelius had anchored his meditation on turning suffering into strength in the same premise:.

Sources indicate that be like a headland: the waves beat against it continuously, but it stands fast and around it the boiling water dies down. “It’s my rotten luck that this has happened to me.” On the contrary, “It’s my good luck that, although this has happened to me, I still feel no distress, since I’m unbruised by the present and unconcerned about the future.” What happened could have happened to anyone, but not everyone could have carried on without letting it distress him.

Here, the Stoic perspective converges with the Buddhist, best articulated by Pema Chödrön in her timeless field guide to transformation through trying times:.

Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over to annihilation can that which is indestructible be found in us.

According to recent reports, and that is the thing about rock bottom: Not only does it hold, but it is there you discover the part of you that also holds — the bedrock of your being unassailable by all the loss, all the failure, all the frivolities of chance. Orwell, being neither a Stoic nor a Buddhist, understood the universality of his experience. “It is a fairly trivial story,” he writes at the end of his memoir — trivial because its essence is so common, no matter the guise; trivial because it touches an elemental truth: The relief of rock bottom is not that you have sunk to it but that, having survived it, you can only rise.

Sources indicate that the manuscript of Orwell’s memoir was twice rejected, including by T.S. Eliot at Faber & Faber. In a fit of despair, Orwell tossed it into his friend Mabel’s garbage bin. She fished it out and, without his knowledge, took it to a literary agent she knew. We could say that the rest is history, but the selective collective memory we call history is an erasure machine for the myriad failures behind every success, for the rock bottom that is so often — so much oftener than our culture likes to admit — the springboard for the redemption of our suffering.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “In disputes upon moral or scientific points,” Arthur Martine counseled in his magnificent 1866 guide to the art of conversation, “let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a latest discovery.” Of course, this isn’t what happens most of the time when we argue, both online and off, but especially when we deploy the artillery of our righteousness from behind the comfortable shield of the keyboard. That form of “criticism” — which is really a menace of reacting rather than responding — is worthy of Mark Twain’s memorable remark that “the critic’s symbol should be the tumble-bug: he deposits his egg in somebody else’s dung, otherwise he could not hatch it.” But it needn’t be this way — there are ways to be critical while remaining charitable, of aiming not to “conquer” but to “come at truth,” not to be right at all costs but to understand and advance the collective understanding.

Daniel Dennett (March 28, 1942–April 19, 2024), whom artificial intelligence pioneer Marvin Minsky has called “our best current philosopher” and “the next Bertrand Russell,” poses an apt question that probes some of the basic tendencies and dynamics of today’s everyone-is-a-critic culture: “Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?”.

Industry observers note that in Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking (public library) — the same fantastic volume that gave us Dennett on the dignity and art-science of making mistakes — he offers what he calls “the best antidote [for the] tendency to caricature one’s opponent”: a list of rules formulated decades ago by the legendary social psychologist and game theorist Anatol Rapoport, best-known for originating the famous tit-for-tat strategy of game theory. Dennett synthesizes the steps:.

How to compose a successful critical commentary:.

If only the same code of conduct could be applied to critical commentary online, particularly to the indelible inferno of comments.

But rather than a naively utopian, Pollyannaish approach to debate, Dennett points out this is actually a sound psychological strategy that accomplishes one key thing: It transforms your opponent into a more receptive audience for your criticism or dissent, which in turn helps advance the discussion.

Compare and contrast with Susan Sontag’s three steps to refuting any argument, and treat yourself to Dennett’s wholly excellent Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking.

Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature

📅 2026-06-30 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Sources indicate that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast. He’s spent years building everything from crypto … More about Mikhail ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sources indicate that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

We know that right now, a senior engineer is shipping a checkout flow they “built” in a single afternoon. AI assistant does the heavy lifting, happy path runs clean, and a rotating chevron spins on the order summary. Two weeks later, engineering gets a notice from customer support: a blind customer using a screen reader can’t complete the purchase because the “Pay Now” control is a with a click handler. No role. Not focusable. Not working.

It has been revealed that that gap — between code that runs and a product people can actually use — is becoming one of the defining engineering challenges of the AI era. Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable.

Accessibility sits right in the middle of that problem.

Recent findings suggest that this is not an article about compliance checklists or end-of-project audits. It’s about engineering systems. Specifically, why accessibility should be treated as an operational capability — alongside privacy, security, reliability, and observability — and what that looks like in practice.

Sources indicate that for years, the default way to “do” accessibility was the one-time, audit-only approach: hire a firm, get a list of 200 findings, fix some of them, file the report. A lot of teams have now moved beyond this model — and the reason is worth looking into.

Sources indicate that audits do matter. For sales, procurement, governance — they’re essential. When a buyer asks for a VPAT or an ACR, you need one. When legal asks if you’re meeting requirements, you need documentation. Audits serve those purposes well.

But audits don’t help you build accessible features during sprint planning. Audits can cost points during a sprint. They don’t catch problems before merge requests. They don’t scale with deployment velocity. The mistake, essentially, is tackling accessibility as a snapshot when you really need constant monitoring. Six months after the audit, the product has shipped dozens of releases, multiple newly introduced features, and a redesigned nav. The report is now fiction. Compliance is not a state you reach — it’s a state you maintain, and complexity fights you the whole way.

The WebAIM Million report, which scans the top one million home pages every year, found that 95.9% of pages had detectable WCAG failures in its 2026 run, with an average of 56.1 errors per page. The number of page elements jumped more than 20% in a single year, likely driven by AI-enabled development and ‘vibe coding’ — and more elements mean more places to break. Accessibility debt behaves exactly like technical debt: every inaccessible component you ship becomes a future remediation project, and the interest compounds.

Any strategy that treats accessibility as a periodic event rather than a continuous property of the system is going to lose.

With the scale at which teams now generate UI, the gap doesn’t just persist; it multiplies.

Start with how fast this arrived. In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” — a way of working where you “fully give in to the vibes” and “forget that the code even exists”. You describe intent, the model generates, you accept the diffs without reading them. It was meant for weekend projects. It did not stay there. Y Combinator reported that 25% of its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated.

Models don’t land on non-semantic markup by accident — three forces push them there. Most React code on GitHub uses non-semantic “soup”, so that’s what the models learn. Human reviewers and evaluators judge output visually, so the feedback loop rewards looks, not semantics. And is fewer tokens than , so absent a constraint, the model takes the cheap path.

In a recent development, here’s the thing about AI-generated UI: it’s inaccessible by default. Not occasionally — by default. A developer writing in Frontend Masters tested AI-generated React components across multiple tools and documented the pattern. A typical AI-generated sidebar had ten distinct accessibility failures in twenty-nine lines: no landmark, no heading, no list structure, elements with click handlers instead of buttons, no aria-expanded, no keyboard handling, and unlabeled icons. The accessibility tree — the structure screen readers actually read — came back as flat, unstructured text. “Same pixels” as the author put it. “One is a door. The other is a painting of a door”.

According to recent reports, now connect this to security, because the two failures come from the same root. Veracode’s 2025 GenAI Code Security Report tested large language models across dozens of coding tasks and found that a large fraction of AI-generated code introduced security vulnerabilities — including OWASP Top 10 flaws. Cross-site scripting failures were particularly common, and security performance did not meaningfully improve with newer, larger models. The matter wasn’t model intelligence. It was process: developers generating code without specifying security constraints and accepting output without systematic verification.

Recent findings suggest that the same shortcut that skips the security review skips the accessibility review. At scale, AI won’t close the accessibility gap — it has industrialized the very thing that creates it.

Recent findings suggest that the fix is not to ban AI. Your developers are already using it. The fix is to constrain it and verify it — to treat AI as a very fast teammate who always needs guardrails.

This is usually where someone claims, “Guardrails? Sounds great, but they will slow us down.”.

In practice, the opposite tends to be true.

According to recent reports, shift-left is the entire DevOps thesis, and it applies cleanly here. An accessibility concern caught during design review is a comment. The same issue found in production is a remediation project.

In a recent development, catching an accessibility matter as a component is built takes minutes. Fixing one after the fact — discovering it in an audit, diagnosing the root cause, restructuring the markup, applying the necessary fix, writing tests — can easily take hours. Multiply that across hundreds of findings from a late-stage audit, and you have weeks of unplanned work that earlier automated checks — whether in design reviews, development workflows, or CI — could have prevented.

Teams that integrate accessibility into everyday workflows avoid the expensive surprises: emergency audits, remediation sprints, procurement blockers, and redesigns that quietly break core user journeys. Accessibility doesn’t reduce velocity. Unexpected work reduces velocity. In-flow accessibility is one way of eliminating unexpected work.

The organizations that scale accessibility successfully do not rely on heroes. They rely on systems.

According to recent reports, the highest-leverage place to start is the design system. One accessible component can be reused thousands of times. The GOV.UK Design System is a useful example: components undergo both automated and manual testing using assistive technologies such as JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack. The team is explicit about the limits of automation and supplements tooling with user testing involving people with disabilities. They’re equally clear that using the design system doesn’t “magically” make a service accessible; it just gives you a higher starting point.

Recent findings suggest that accessibility becomes infrastructure. That’s the lesson.

From there, it moves into the engineering workflow:.

Finally, accessibility becomes enforceable through automation:.

At that point, accessibility stops depending on memory and starts depending on the process. It becomes part of your platform.

A few implementation patterns consistently show up in teams that do this well.

Industry observers note that instead of fixing accessibility after generation, bake requirements directly into tooling through Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, or repository-level standards. Tell the model to use semantic HTML. Tell it when to use buttons versus links. Tell it to expose the state and labels correctly. Models follow persistent constraints far more reliably than one-off prompts.

Recent findings suggest that comboboxes, menus, tabs, modals, and similar controls routinely become accessibility hotspots. Libraries such as Radix UI, React Aria, and Headless UI already solve many of these problems. The scalable approach is not about repeatedly implementing accessibility correctly. It’s inheriting accessible behavior from well-tested primitives.

According to recent reports, focus order, labels, heading hierarchy, and interaction states should be specified before implementation begins. If accessibility requirements are absent from the design artifact, they are often absent from the final product. A simple memo at design handoff — what is the tab order, what are the labels, what happens on error — removes a huge amount of guesswork later.

None of these patterns is exotic. They’re just DevOps and platform thinking applied to accessibility.

Engineering leaders rarely prioritize accessibility solely because of regulations. But regulations, procurement requirements, user retention, and product quality all point in the same direction.

Sources indicate that legal pressure continues to increase. Digital accessibility lawsuits in the United States have stayed in the thousands per year, and they are not limited to large enterprises. The European Accessibility Act is now enforceable across the EU, applying to e‑commerce, banking, ticketing, telecoms, and more, regardless of where the company is headquartered. The message is clear: accessibility is no longer a “nice-to-have” in the eyes of regulators.

Sources indicate that but compliance is only part of the story. The bigger story is the market you leave on the table. The World Economic Forum (December 2023) estimates that the world’s 1.3 billion people with disabilities, “along with their friends and family, has a spending power of $13 trillion”; disabled consumers alone control roughly $8 trillion in annual disposable income, per the Valuable 500.

In the UK alone, the Click-Away Pound Report 2019 found the “Click-Away Pound has risen to £17.1 billion” — more than 4.9 million customers with access needs who abandon inaccessible sites and spend elsewhere, up almost 45% from £11.75 billion in 2016. People don’t file a bug report. They leave and buy from a competitor.

Sources indicate that there is also a procurement reality that turns accessibility from a cost into a moat. If you sell B2B or to government, you will increasingly be asked for proof of accessibility — VPATs/ACRs or equivalent documentation. According to Level Access’s Seventh Annual State of Digital Accessibility Report, 75% of organizations now require proof of accessibility at least most of the time when purchasing digital products — essentially unchanged from 74% in the previous report, but with a notable shift towards stricter enforcement, as those that always require it rose from 27% to 31%. A strong ACR accelerates the sales cycle; a weak one, or none at all, creates redlines that stall or kill it. For some buyers, this is a hard requirement before your product can even enter evaluation. A strong accessibility story accelerates the sales cycle. A weak one creates redlines that stall or kill it.

Step back and the deeper pattern is clear: accessibility is a proxy for engineering maturity. A team that ships semantic HTML, manages focus, exposes state correctly, and tests it in CI is a team that has its house in order. The same discipline that produces an accessible component produces a maintainable, testable, less buggy one.

For dev and product leaders, that’s the real business case: accessibility work is platform work. It pays off every time a feature ships faster and more smoothly, with less rework, than it otherwise would have.

If you take one thing from this, make it this: accessibility doesn’t come from an audit, a hero, or a heroic remediation sprint before launch. It comes from systems.

It has been revealed that an accessible design system so components start right. A Definition of Done so they stay right. Automated testing and CI gates so regressions fail the build. Governance, so someone owns it. Guardrails for AI-assisted development so your fastest tool stops being your biggest liability.

None of those practices is particularly glamorous. That’s exactly why they work. They’re the same kinds of boring, reliable systems you already trust for security, reliability, and performance.

But there’s one thing no tool on that list can do. No linter, no automated scanner run, no dashboard will ever tell you what it’s actually like to use your product as a blind person with a screen reader, or to navigate your checkout with a keyboard because a tremor makes a mouse inoperable. So build the systems — you need them, and they’re the only way accessibility survives contact with a real release schedule. But test with real customers with disabilities regularly. The first time you sit behind someone using JAWS to fight through a form your team thought was “done”, something changes. The tooling tells you whether you passed. A real person tells you whether it actually works.

According to recent reports, accessibility is not a feature. It’s an operational capability. Treat it that way, and you get something dev and product leaders already care about: a faster, safer, more reliable way to ship software.

The Only Three Distinctions Between People

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It may be that consciousness evolved to sieve the relevant from the incomprehensible allness of all there is, to parse the world into concepts and find an organizing principle for the chaos of them.
  • Two centuries ago, Nathaniel Hawthorne (July 4, 1804–May 19, 1864) offered a pithy, powerful antidote to this double-edged instinct.
  • Sources indicate that in a notebook entry from the autumn of 1836, penned shortly after his moving meditation on how not to waste your life, Hawthorne proposes a revision of our standard classification system for humanity — one that would rehumanize us with the simple awareness that what binds us is infinitely stronger than what divides us or by what affiliations we divide ourselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It may be that consciousness evolved to sieve the relevant from the incomprehensible allness of all there is, to parse the world into concepts and find an organizing principle for the chaos of them. Our cognitive inheritance is a restless yearning to fathom how things cohere and where they belong, a yearning we have given shape to in laws and labels, weights and balances, hierarchies and categories. It has served us well, this instinct to categorize in order to contain, giving us music, the laws of planetary motion, and democracy. But it also pulsates beneath every ism we have ever invented, beneath every stereotype and every genocide, beneath every algorithm that reduces us to variables then adds them up to sell the sum of who we are, beneath all the parcels of preconception we trade daily and mistake the barter a for a genuine encounter with one another.

Two centuries ago, Nathaniel Hawthorne (July 4, 1804–May 19, 1864) offered a pithy, powerful antidote to this double-edged instinct.

Sources indicate that in a notebook entry from the autumn of 1836, penned shortly after his moving meditation on how not to waste your life, Hawthorne proposes a revision of our standard classification system for humanity — one that would rehumanize us with the simple awareness that what binds us is infinitely stronger than what divides us or by what affiliations we divide ourselves. He writes:.

A fresh classification of society is to be instituted. Instead of rich and poor, high and low, they are to be classed, — First, by their sorrows: for instance, whenever there are any, whether in fair mansion or hovel, who are mourning the loss of relations and friends, and who wear black, whether the cloth be coarse or superfine, they are to make one class. Secondly, all who have the same maladies, whether they lie under damask canopies or on straw pallets or in the wards of hospitals, they are to form one class. Thirdly, all who are guilty of the same sins, whether the world knows them or not; whether they languish in prison, looking forward to the gallows, or walk honored among men, they also form a class. Then proceed to generalize and classify the whole world together, as none can claim utter exemption from either sorrow, sin, or disease; and if they could, yet Death, like a great parent, comes and sweeps all through one darksome portal, — all his children.

What a magnificent way to remember that down where the spirit meets the bone, we are all facing the same struggle: to feel safe, to feel seen, to wrest some meaning and some marvel from the ephemeral bewilderment of being alive.
