Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams

📅 2026-11-12 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it.

Recent findings suggest that A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered.

Sources indicate that rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was.

The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles.

Recent findings suggest that every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply.

An AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together.

We can call that the break-even line. Returns to users come in three forms:.

Industry observers note that for example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool indicates the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. That puts the feature above the break-even line.

It has been revealed that four questions can help your team locate the break-even line before design work starts. Each one produces a design condition the brief can act on.

According to recent reports, these questions do not replace the build decision. Funding, strategy, and existing commitments all weigh on that, and four questions cannot see any of it.

Run through all four questions together, since no single question settles the concern alone. Do it while the feature is still a proposal, before anyone sinks weeks into design. You will also need at least one person who does the task for a living, such as a loan officer, analyst, or benefits specialist. They do not have to sit in the roadmap meeting, and a short conversation tells you where the mental effort actually sits and whether the feature would help or add work.

Industry observers note that count everything the task asks of the user: the thinking, the clicking, and the checking they will owe once AI is involved. Fewer clicks proves nothing on its own, because a feature can cut clicks and still leave the person working harder. Write down the cost even when it goes up, since Question 2 may find a return that pays for it.

It has been revealed that A loan officer reading 40 financial disclosures to find the three that conflict with lending policy is thinking hard, and AI that surfaces those conflicts cuts that demand directly. Compare that with typing a loan number into a tracking system, which costs a few seconds and almost no thought. Pre-filling that field relocates the cost instead of removing it, because the officer now checks what the machine entered. Conventional wisdom indicates to automate the repetitive and monotonous tasks, and the pre-filled field is where that advice misfires. In this example:.

You can find the tasks worth automating by comparing total effort before and after. Count the checking the user inherits on the after side.

It has been revealed that who the user is matters as much as what the task is. One feature can clear the line for a junior analyst and fall short for a senior one. Hand a junior analyst an AI-drafted risk summary, and they gain a starting point they lack the pattern library to produce on their own. A senior analyst, however, reads that same summary against the analysis already formed in their head, spends four minutes doing it, and learns nothing.

A finding like that tells you who to ship to. Scope the addition to the group it serves.

In a recent development, compare the AI approach against the user’s current method, including the spreadsheets and workarounds they built for themselves. Genuine ambiguity is one reason AI comes out ahead when someone explores options, produces a starting point, or looks for patterns too numerous to spot by hand. Scale, speed, and consistency across a group of people doing the same job are three more. A fourth is catching what the current method reliably misses, which is how the fraud screening tool earns its place. The advantage disappears once the user has a practiced route to a known answer.

Sources indicate that for example, an HR team building a succession planning tool finds the answer running both ways inside one product. Using AI to surface internal candidates whose skill combinations nobody would think to search for wins on ambiguity and scale together, since no single right answer exists and manual review of that search space would take weeks. Drafting the notification email after someone picks a candidate loses to the method already in place. The format is familiar, the writing takes two minutes, and the person sending it holds firm opinions about tone. The candidate search earns the addition. The email draft layers an interaction onto a task that runs fine without one.

The nature of the input and the shape of the output are separate decisions. A task can hold genuine ambiguity and still call for a structured visual result instead of a conversational one. Pair this audit with a modality evaluation for the output side.

Every AI system makes mistakes. The question is whether your user will notice. Start with how visible the error is. Then weigh what it costs when nobody catches it, and whether the user still has the skill to catch it. Question 1 asks what checking costs. This one asks whether checking is even possible.

Error visibility varies enormously, and product teams tend to estimate it badly. For example, an AI trip planner that suggests a museum on the day it closes produces an invisible error, because nothing in the output looks wrong. The traveler finds out while standing outside a locked door in Tokyo. Compare that with a suggested flight that departs before the connecting flight lands, where the contradiction sits right there on the screen.

In a recent development, automation bias makes the invisible cases worse. Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey (2010) reviewed decades of human factors research showing that people defer to automated output even when that output is wrong, across aviation, medicine, and process control. Trust climbs fast, and rarely as a conscious decision. Once it does, users stop applying the scrutiny that would catch the mistake.

It has been revealed that map the error surface, meaning the ways this feature can be wrong, before design work starts. List the three likeliest error types. Rate each one on visibility to the user and consequence if it slips through. Any combination of low visibility and high consequence becomes a design requirement.

Show customers where the output came from and how the system produced it. That is provenance, and it is what lets trust settle at the right level. People who can see the source, the data behind it, and when it was pulled catch errors more often. Tell the traveler that a restaurant’s hours came from a page cached in March and they know what to check. A confident-sounding paragraph with no source attached leaves them guessing.

In a recent development, letting the routine work go is a real benefit of adding AI. Nobody needs to protect a specialist’s ability to format a citation or an analyst’s ability to total a column by hand, and arguing to preserve skills the technology has absorbed wastes everyone’s time.

It has been revealed that still, the judgment that catches the machine’s mistakes stays exempt from replacement. That judgment makes every other delegation safe, and disuse degrades it like any other skill.

In a recent development, research in radiology shows how fast a suggestion can override a reader’s own judgment. In a 2023 experiment, Thomas Dratsch and colleagues had 27 radiologists read mammograms alongside what they were told was an AI system (a simulation created solely for the experiment). The radiologists worked through a 10-image training set where the suggested category was always correct, then 40 more mammograms with incorrect suggestions planted in 12 of them. The result showed how incorrect AI suggestions damaged diagnostic accuracy at every experience level. The most experienced readers, averaging 15 years, assigned the correct category 82.3% of the time when the suggestion was right and 45.5% of the time when it was wrong, while the least experienced group fell from 79.7% to 19.8%. Experience softened the effect without preventing it. A year of deferring to the same system, with the judgment it replaced sitting unused, leaves a reader in a weaker position than the one these radiologists started from.

In a recent development, question 3 looks at your user today. Extend the same test 12 months forward and you arrive at Question 4. Teams that answer the first and skip the second read the resulting failures as a quality problem in the model, when the cause is the human judgment they took out of daily use.

Ask whether this user could judge the quality of the output 12 months from now if the feature vanished tomorrow. When the answer is no, the design needs a mechanism that keeps verification skill in use. Periodic blind review works well and costs little, with the user forming a judgment before seeing what the AI produced. Rotating a share of cases off AI assistance does a similar job, as does a weekly comparison between machine output and a human-produced version.

Table 1 below gathers the four questions, the signals pointing each way, and the condition each one produces.

In a recent development, table 1: The AI Addition Decision Matrix. Clear answers across all four questions point toward building the feature as proposed. A poor answer on Question 1 calls for a design condition or a change in scope, unless Question 2 finds a return that covers the cost. Questions 2 and 4 work the same way without that exception. A poor answer on Question 3 can stop the build.

Sources indicate that put the conditions in the design brief, where they become project requirements. Teams reduce AI features to yes or no because roadmap reviews demand it, and that throws away everything the audit found. A feature that answers well on Questions 1 and 2 and poorly on Question 3 proceeds only with provenance built in. Write that in on day one. Requirements that arrive at the end read as polish, and teams cut polish when timelines slip.

Industry observers note that let’s return to the insurer scenario from our opening. The first version of the tool fails Question 1. Writing a determination takes sustained thought, and the AI that produces the draft moves that effort into verification without reducing the total. An hour with the four questions would surface that before the first version reaches design.

Question 2 points in the same direction. Appeals determinations follow a familiar structure, and specialists reach the answer through a practiced route. The ambiguity in the task sits earlier, in finding which provisions and prior decisions apply.

In a recent development, question 3 raises the stakes. A wrong determination affects someone’s medical coverage, and an error buried in fluent prose stays invisible until the next appeal arrives. That answer produces the provenance requirement in the second version, which cites the source document and retrieval date for every provision it surfaces.

Question 4 explains why the second version holds up. Specialists still write every determination, so the judgment that evaluates the retrieved material stays in daily use. Keeping version one would train specialists for a year to approve text they no longer have the practice to assess.

AI-generated meeting summaries sit inside products that millions of people open every day, and the audit reaches a different answer for them.

In a recent development, on Question 1, a summary removes the work of writing notes and adds the work of checking whether it attributed a decision to the right person. Total effort drops for the participant who never took notes. For the person who always took the notes and circulated them, the trade is closer, and the verification lands on them. That split is exactly what Question 1 is built to surface.

Sources indicate that question 2 compares the summary against someone typing while half-listening, which produces patchy notes. A summary beats that on completeness and on consistency from meeting to meeting, so the feature clears this question for most teams.

According to recent reports, A summary that assigns a commitment to the wrong person looks exactly like a correct one, and nobody rereads the transcript to check. On Question 3, low visibility and real consequence together turn into a requirement for a linked source timestamp behind every action item.

According to recent reports, the feature clears Question 4, and the design needs no mechanism. Nobody loses a skill worth protecting by giving up meeting notes, and the participants keep making every decision the summary records.

In a recent development, two clear answers, one segment finding, and one condition. The timestamps ship with the feature, and the habitual note-taker is the segment the team checks after launch.

You can run this before the next AI feature reaches your roadmap.

Everett Rogers (2003) called this pro-innovation bias, the assumption that latest capability means progress before anyone verifies the benefit, and competitive pressure turns a rival’s announcement into an internal mandate. An hour of structured questions gives your team a way to answer that pressure.

Audit results land badly when a designer presents them as reasons the feature should not exist. The conditions are the useful output, so bring those into the product review.

Start by naming the segment the feature serves, which makes the answer a yes for someone. Hand over the error surface as a requirement with a cost attached. A product manager can act on a request for timestamps behind every attributed decision, and nobody can act on a worry that users might not trust the output. Then offer the change in scope without waiting to be asked. A version that surfaces the provisions instead of writing the determination is a smaller build with a better adoption story, and that framing moves a roadmap conversation forward.

A sentence that works out loud: We think this clears the bar for junior analysts and adds a verification step for senior analysts, so we would scope it to onboarding and revisit the rest next quarter.

Sources indicate that the attention a person can spend in a working day stays fixed no matter how good your model gets. Before the next feature reaches design, write down what it will cost the person doing the work and which of the three returns pays for it. With both answers in hand, your team can walk into the roadmap review with a scope to propose.

AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

📅 2026-11-17 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • It has been revealed that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

Sources indicate that lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up.

Sources indicate that we asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most noted they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage.

These results point to a two-speed workflow. AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible?

Accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now.

This matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor.

Industry observers note that so how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace?

We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently.

Here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge shows up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training, communication, and a culture of accessibility.

According to recent reports, A quick caveat: This is survey data, so it only indicates correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore.

And it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize challenges. They were also nearly three times as likely to say it helps them tackle accessibility more proactively in development.

In other words, AI works best as an amplifier of a strong program. With context, testing, environments, and guardrails in place, agents can take on a large share of the work from drafting through to operations, and much of the time lost to waiting and handoffs goes away. People stay responsible for deciding what to build and for approving what ships.

So let me ask you: When it comes to accessibility, where does human judgment sit in your workflow today?

Not sure? Here’s a quick way to find out.

Pick a feature you shipped recently and trace it from the first Figma frame to production. Mark every moment a person decided whether it would work for someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, or their browser at 400% zoom.

How many marks did you get? If most of them cluster at the end of creation, you’re likely heading to one of two places: You’ll either ship accessibility barriers or spend the time you saved upstream fixing them later, when they’re harder and costlier to fix.

Here’s how to avoid both outcomes by building the right accessibility checks and judgment calls into the work your team is already doing.

In a recent development, as AI takes on more work, people need to stay involved at three points: finding issues, fixing them, and documenting the evidence. Each one plugs into a step your team already takes, like a handoff, a pull request, or a review, so nothing latest gets added to the timeline, and accessibility keeps pace with the work that’s in motion.

Recent findings suggest that context fades fast. Put the first judgment checkpoints as close to the creation work as you can:.

According to recent reports, found the matter? Great. Fix it while it’s fresh. When complications end up as tickets, make sure the context travels with them. They should carry the element, the repro, the related WCAG criterion, a suggested fix, and the PR link, so context doesn’t leak.

The worst time to start gathering evidence is when somebody’s asking for it.

Industry observers note that every check, fix, and judgment call throughout the process described above should ideally leave a trail. A fix isn’t done until something fails if the issue comes back. Ask your AI assistant to write the regression test with the fix and put the finding link and any judgment call in the PR description. That’s the receipt.

A passing test highlights a known glitch hasn’t returned. It doesn’t show the experience works. For what automation can’t cover, add a short note to the PR: what you tested, with which assistive technology, and any judgment calls you made.

In a recent development, AI has given digital creation a speed boost, but broadly speaking, validating the work hasn’t kept pace. Closing that gap isn’t about adopting more AI in more places or abandoning the toolset that helped make your team faster.

According to our data, the opportunity in front of teams is to build the practice around that toolset, so that human judgment is flagged, embedded, and acted on earlier, and more often.

Industry observers note that we’ve only scratched the surface of what our data tells us about AI and accessibility. If you’re curious about what else we found, check out the 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. There’s plenty more to unpack.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a latest chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman.
  • Recent findings suggest that “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a latest chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman. Accompanied by an endowment to establish the institution’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design, the donation will help broaden the museum’s collection and increase its scholarly contributions.

Recent findings suggest that “This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper. “It significantly expands our understanding of art history, bringing together artistic expression and material and technical innovation.”.

According to recent reports, the gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. The collection traces the medium’s evolution from the sinuous forms of Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts to the streamlined aesthetics of Art Deco and Modernism. Early 20th-century examples by Tiffany Studios, Émile Gallé and the renowned studio Daum demonstrate how artists pushed glass beyond traditional decorative applications.

In a recent development, daum Frères, Lamp, around 1905. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

According to recent reports, the works also chart the emergence of studio glass as an independent discipline in the post-war period. Additional artists with works in the donation include Dale Chihuly, whose gravity-defying installations are in museums worldwide, as well as the studio glass pioneer Toots Zynsky and the well-known Canadian American artist Laura Donefer.

A selection of pieces from the collection is right now on view in the NGC’s European galleries (until 30 April 2027). Highlights of the installation include Edward Hald’s The Fireworks Bowl (around 1921), alongside architectural works by Tiffany and Frank Lloyd Wright.

“Harvey Littleton’s Red Crossed Form (1990) is another notable work that reflects the development of studio glass as an independent artistic medium,” states Anabelle Kienle Ponka, the NGC’s senior curator of European, American and Asian Art. “The presentation brings together very different approaches to glass, from the decorative traditions of the early 20th century to the formal and technical experimentation of contemporary artists.”.

According to recent reports, tiffany Studios, Lamp, around 1900. Collection of Charles and the late Andrea Bronfman Photo: NGC.

Industry observers note that the international scope of the donation highlights the exchange of technical traditions, particularly the influence of Venetian glassmaking on successive generations of artists, Kienle Ponka notes. Together, the works demonstrate the medium’s versatility across sculpture, architecture and ornamentation.

In a recent development, equally significant for the NGC is the accompanying endowment, which will fund the museum’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design. The NGC has not shared the sum of the endowment, but notes that the post will support research, exhibitions and future acquisitions, establishing a foundation for sustained institutional engagement with the field.

According to recent reports, “[The donation’s] significance extends well beyond this gift,” Bélisle says. “The position will allow us to pursue further acquisitions, develop exhibitions and scholarship, and build relationships with artists and institutions.”.

Installation view of works by Lino Tagliapietra and Harvey Littleton from the Bronfman Glass Collection, National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa, until 30 April 2027. Photo: National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa.

It has been revealed that the donation builds on a long history of the Bronfman family’s philanthropy in Canada's cultural sector. “My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Charles Bronfman said in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”.

The NGC has received other transformative gifts in recent years, including a 2025 donation of 61 contemporary works valued at C$22.8m ($16.8m) from collector Bob Rennie and his family. “The Bronfman gift is significant in a different way,” Bélisle says. “Its importance lies not only in the quality and range of the works, but also in the accompanying endowment, which will provide the expertise and resources to develop decorative arts and design as a sustained area of collecting and scholarship.”.

BUCK gives conservation nonprofit Tula Global a brand identity built on a pixel spark, topographic lines and vivid color.

It has been revealed that the mark is a spark made of square pixels, a small t built from the same blocks at its core. BUCK pairs that precise grid with topographic contour lines that read as terrain at survey scale and as fingerprints up close, so the whole system ties land to people in one gesture. The palette does the rest of the talking. Deep forest green carries the wordmark, burnt orange and lime cut through it, and lilac, sky blue and burgundy fill out the range, so every panel lands somewhere different while the grid holds it together.

In a recent development, the wordmark stays lowercase and rounded, tula set small beside the spark, and the spark itself doubles as the letterform, so the name and the symbol read as one unit from a cap brim to a billboard. Headlines run large in the same rounded grotesque, set tight in short lines that stack like the pixel blocks, and the line that carries the whole offer reads plain: Six months. Real skills. Direct pathways to employment.

Small caps kickers label each section, THE TULA MODEL, OUR GRADUATES, OUR MISSION, in a lighter weight that lets the big lines breathe. The symbol grid becomes the layout grid. Panels split into halves and thirds along the same pixel rhythm, contour lines run across the joins, and the custom data visualizations sit inside the same structure, so a deck slide and a poster share one set of rules.

The system earns its keep in the field. Outdoor signs carry the wordmark and the mission in orange and cream, framed posters hang on brick, and the Tula Model booklet pairs green hills with lime contour lines. The mark travels just as well on cloth, embroidered in orange thread on a burgundy cap and printed large on the back of a field vest, then out to a white van running the green wordmark down its flank.

On screen the same language holds, with the model page stacking big type, field photography and contour panels on a phone. Documentary photography of the training and the survey work sits beside the graphics rather than under them, and the custom data system turns the program into charts and maps that read at a glance. Nothing in the kit is decoration. Every panel, poster and garment repeats the grid, the lines and the color, so the identity feels built, not applied.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Bolivia’s oldest churches, known as the “Sistine Chapel of the Andes” due to its impressive murals, is nearing completion of a conservation project focused on its roofs, stone buttresses and adobe walls—a process that began in May.

The US Department of State’s Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP) financed the work at the Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas church, located in the Andes mountains at almost 4,000m above sea level. Approximately 170km west of the city of Oruro, the church was declared a National Monument in 1960.

“The Curahuara church has great value because of its paintings, so it’s essential that the roof is in good condition to prevent leaks that could compromise the murals,” Josefina Matas, the architect in charge of the project, tells The Art Newspaper. This work follows restoration that took place more than a decade ago, funded by the German embassy in La Paz.

It has been revealed that the restoration team has had to learn the church’s unique roof-building technique from locals, placing straw on top of hollow cane mats using a method that makes it more resilient. Hollow cane is hard to find in the highlands, so they needed to bring it in from Bolivia’s southernmost region of Tarija.

Working on the church’s new roofs Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia.

Sources indicate that during the previous restoration, corrugated metal sheets had been added to extend the lifespan of the roofs, which cover 800 sq. m. This time, workers replaced the damaged sections. The project was delayed because of proteststhat blocked roads across the country in May and June, preventing the arrival of materials and postponing its completion by one month—from the end of October to the end of November.

Sources indicate that built by Augustinians between the late 16th and early 17th centuries, the church houses paintings of the Nativity, the Last Supper, the Crucifixion and the Last Judgment in a display of religious syncretism. “It’s a complete catechesis,” Matas says of the murals, which were made using natural dyes and finished in 1777.

There are also representations of the apostle Santiago (James), the church’s patron saint. Local Indigenous people identified him with Illapa, the Inca god of thunder. The style of the paintings ranges from Mannerism to 18th-century Baroque, with depictions of birds and flowers—an example of mestizo art.

According to recent reports, “It’s very striking when you enter the church, because there isn’t any empty space,” Matas indicates. “Everything is painted.” The paintings even cover the baptistery and sacristy. “Most of the churches in the region have murals. Here, they have been well preserved,” she adds.

Restoration underway at Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas Courtesy US Embassy in Bolivia.

Industry observers note that the building has a single entrance through a side wall, similar to other churches in the area, and is surrounded by an atrium with two gates. “Indigenous people weren’t used to entering the building for religious activities, so the atrium was spacious enough to accommodate those who wanted to be evangelised,” Matas says.

Recent findings suggest that the bishop of Oruro, Krzysztof Białasik, was the one who submitted the restoration project to compete for US funding. Since 2001, the AFCP has financed more than 30 projects in Bolivia, including the restoration of colonial paintings, the protection of Baroque musical manuscripts and the creation of a digital catalogue—including archaeological artefacts, pre-Columbian textiles and colonial art—available to customs services to curb the illicit trafficking of these goods.

To celebrate the completion of the conservation of the church, a mass will be held in Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas with the bishop and the apostolic nuncio on 15 December.

Dinamo rebuilt early-web Arial from scratch for Are.na, turning invisible typography craft into ABC Areal and releasing the family free.

Sources indicate that are.na spent a full year rewriting its back-end code without changing a single visible pixel on screen. Nobody noticed, and nobody sent congratulations, yet Are.naâs Cab told Dinamoâs Johannes there was real satisfaction in fixing what sits underneath. That quiet pride sparked a tricky typography brief. Are.na had used Arial for fifteen years and didnât want a dramatic latest voice; the default sans still felt like a less snobby cousin to Helvetica. Their breakthrough came from Kristin Lucasâs performance piece Refresh, in which she legally changed her own name to the exact same name just to start over. Berlin-based foundry Dinamo took that cue literally and redrew Arial from the ground up as ABC Areal â releasing the entire family for free one year after it went live on Are.na.

Industry observers note that unlike print revivals pulled from old books or posters, Arial was born digital. Commissioned by IBM in 1982 from Monotype designers Robin Nicholas and Patricia Saunders, it landed on Windows 3.1 in 1992 before Microsoft picked Arial 2.82 in 1996 as a core web font. Dinamo treated that thirty-year-old software like a dig site, partnering with technology archivists to boot legacy machines and capture screenshots of the original web release as a tracing blueprint. The payoff indicates immediately in the side-by-side lowercase a outline chart. Arial 2.82 packs clustered, uneven anchor points along its upper arch and bowl, whereas Areal 1.0 strips that clutter down to clean BÃ©zier extrema without disturbing the familiar slanted top terminal. Those rebuilt forms play out across four retro Dinamo Font Browser windows framed like classic desktop write tools, scaling from dense character strings up to display capitals with Are.naâs double-asterisk glyph tucked into the title bars and punctuation rows.

It has been revealed that the revival doesnât stop at tidying up old curves. Dinamoâs wireframe designspace cube maps ABC Arealâs typography across three axes: Weight, Slant, and Proportion, stretching the character set smoothly from proportional spacing into monospaced territory. On the family overview sheet, that structure expands into eighteen cuts split across ABC Areal, ABC Areal Semi-Mono, and ABC Areal Mono, each carrying Regular, Medium, and Bold weights alongside matching italics. A clean three-circle Venn diagram sums up the commission without a slogan, placing Are.na, Dinamo, and Arial around Areal in the center. Itâs a working set of everyday typography built for dense research blocks, quiet headings, and anyone who wants a sharper, free alternative to the webâs oldest default.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier. The entire historic centre of Odesa was added to Unesco’s list of endangered World Heritage sites in 2023.

At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.

“Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.

Recent findings suggest that the neo-Byzantine St Volodymyr Cathedral, built in the 19th century, is under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), which broke with the Moscow Patriarchate and was granted autocephaly by Constantinople in 2018. Three of Russia’s most famous artists of the 19th century and early 20th century—Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel and Mikhail Nesterov—created religious art for St Volodymyr’s, as did the Ukrainian artist Mykola Pymomenko, a teacher of Kazimir Malevich.

Recent findings suggest that the Austrian embassy, located next-door to St Volodymyr's Cathedral, was also damaged. Kyiv's municipal cultural heritage department published an inventory of damage from the attack, which also includes the embassy of the Netherlands.

A Russian drone was shot down over St Michael’s, which is the headquarters of the OCU, on 19 November.

Industry observers note that berezhna’s post cites the cumulative damage from Russia’s accelerating attacks: “Since the beginning of this year, the number of monuments damaged by Russia has increased by more than a third, and by the end of October it was almost 2,200. Almost 2,700 cultural institutions were also affected.”.

According to recent reports, the minister was in Lutsk, a historic city in northwestern Ukraine, this week to blueprint for a conference marking the 600th anniversary in 2029 of the Congress of Lutsk, which brought together the regional monarchies of the time. A Russian strike on Lutsk in October damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, Cosmogony, a 2,000 sq. m work by the contemporary artist Petro Antyp.

Sources indicate that unesco has condemned the latest attacks, especially on Odesa, “which hit the centre of the city, within the boundaries of the World Heritage property ‘The Historic Centre of Odesa’” and “reportedly caused damage to several heritage buildings, including the Kalio Palace, a monument of national importance,” according to a statement released by the organisation. The Kalio Palace, built in 1834, is attributed to the Swiss Italian architect Giorgio Torricelli.

Sources indicate that the strikes came amid escalating tensions and a diplomatic chasm that appears to be widening. The Russian President Vladimir Putin mentioned this week that the Kremlin would not negotiate any partial ceasefire or deal with Ukraine after it struck and incapacitated the Kerch Bridge linking mainland Russia to Crimea, a symbol of Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014, on 16 and 17 November. At the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed that peace, largely on Russia’s terms, is within reach and reportedly urged European leaders to stop funding weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping signed a “peace declaration” on 20 November at a trilateral summit hosted by Xi in Shenzhen, China.

Sources indicate that A petition to “safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage and artistic integrity” was rolled out last month by the curator Konstantin Akinsha and Bjorn Geldof, the artistic director at Kyiv’s PinchukArtCentre. It calls “for immediate sanctions and the suspension of Russian state participation in international cultural events”. Rapporteur, a Brussels-based policy publication, reported this week that ten European countries are seeking to keep Russia out of the 2027 Architecture Biennale. Russia’s participation in the 2026 Venice Biennale set off a series of protests.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Base Design rebuilds The Huntington brand identity around a sculpted H monogram, a hidden gem idea and green drawn from pigment and plant life.

The Huntington is a library, an art museum and botanical gardens on 200 acres in Southern California, founded in 1919, and most visitors knew only the gardens. Base Design starts from the mark itself. Two flanking pillars in lime green hold a diamond shaped gem at the center, set against a deep green field. The studio calls the idea a hidden gem, treasured, layered, quietly extraordinary, and the mark behaves that way. It never shouts. It sits still and lets the green do the talking, while accents shift like light on a leaf or oil on canvas.

The wordmark is set in a serif with flared terminals, THE HUNTINGTON debossed into a green textured surface so the letters read as much by shadow as by ink. The same voice carries the exhibition posters, where single words stack large and flat. ROSE breaks across four stacked lines in pink, cut-out rose photographs tucked between the letters, on a poster lying in the flower beds. The orchid show poster sets its title in pink and purple over a full-bleed orchid photograph.

Recent findings suggest that the H doubles as a pattern. On the What's On board it repeats in four colourways, orange, green, blue and yellow, each stem holding its gem. A close crop of the mark fills a whole frame with one lime stem and crossbar against dark green, the curve of the pillar edge doing all the work.

According to recent reports, print carries the system. Brochures rest on giant green leaves, their covers carrying the H and the names of the collections. A flat lay of the print suite reveals the orchid show poster, the bonsai collection guide, a portrait exhibition guide and a yellow Stories from the Library sheet, each piece holding the same green and the same serif. The Library Quarterly sits on a leather chair, its cream cover and red masthead quiet against the dark wood around it.

Outside, the system scales up without changing its voice. A dark green wayfinding totem stands among the planting, its directory set in small capitals above the H at the base.

Two exhibition billboards pair portraits with green type, one for Mineo Mizuno, one for Don Bachardy, and the same green runs through the noticeboards.

First Frieze Abu Dhabi proves successful for the region's dealers, despite geopolitical jitters

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) opened to a promising start.
  • It has been revealed that “They’re looking after us very well here,” one established Dubai collector said.
  • In a recent development, like its name, Frieze Abu Dhabi was a mix of two halves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) opened to a promising start. Strong sales were reported across many galleries, and the fair had an energy that spread from the stands to the garden outside at the Manarat Al Saadiyat, where guests lingered for hours over the unlikely combination of pizza and champagne.

It has been revealed that “They’re looking after us very well here,” one established Dubai collector said. “Unlike at other fairs, where we feel pressured to buy, here we can take a breather and reflect on things. The art world is very collegiate in this region and the collectors are here to support.”.

In a recent development, like its name, Frieze Abu Dhabi was a mix of two halves. The successor to the long-standing Abu Dhabi Art fair that has been operating, under various names, in the UAE capital since 2007, the fair is co-run by Frieze Fairs and the UAE government’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT). Accordingly, the event blended elements of Abu Dhabi Art’s programme with those more familiar to Frieze's flagship event in Regent’s Park.

Chief among these is the Ladies’ Day—the day before the public opening that is reserved for Abu Dhabi’s sheikhas—and the pre-bound book of available works that is sent around to the city’s royals.

In a recent development, meanwhile Frieze brought its art fair expertise, giving the fair a better layout and an improved allover experience. “The fair still has its Abu Dhabi Art soul but feels a lot tighter in terms of the number of galleries and the selection,” said Taymour Grahne, whose eponymous gallery moved from New York to London and has now settled in Dubai. Grahne was showing a series of mosaics by the Palestinian artist Ala Younis, which by the opening day had mostly sold.

Industry observers note that most of the galleries’ presentations were rooted in the Wanasa (West Asia, North Africa and South Asia) region. Standout booths included that of the Cairo gallery Art Talks/Kanafani's solo presentation of the Egyptian surrealist Samir Rafi, and the Dubai gallery Ayyam’s booth of the Dutch-Iraqi artist Sadik Kwaish Alfraiji. By the opening day, the Rafi works were about half sold.

Other Dubai galleries, who had a strong showing at the fair, equally did well, with Lawrie Shabibi selling out its marble inlay works by Hamra Abbas by the opening day for $50,000 each; Zawyeh Gallery selling about half of its collages by the Gazan artist Mohammed Joha, which had attracted much attention this year at the Venice Biennale; and Tabari Artspace, which revealed two early works by another artist born in Gaza, Hazem Harb, amidst a group show, also reported selling half their booth. Most artworks were priced in the region of ten-thousands to mid-hundred thousand dollars.

A mix of blue-chip Western galleries were also in attendance. Pace were offering their fresh-to-market, large-scale paintings by the indigenous Australian artist Emily Kame Kngwarreye for between $80,000 to $750,000, although confirmed sales for these works appeared to be slow.

And in the small Frieze Masters section, a 2,000-year-old funerary stele made out of luminous alabaster, taken by a British official from what is now Yemen, was sold by the Mayfair gallerist David Aaron for "seven figures".

Sources indicate that there were also a substantial number of fresh visitors to the fair, including a few starry faces like the tennis star Venus Williams. A smattering of museum heads and curators from the US, Asia and Europe also flew in, such as Michael Govan of Lacma (who was speaking at the fair), Eugene Tan of the Singapore Art Museum, and the Aspen Art Museum’s Nicola Lees, one of a number who brought along a patrons group.

And though the fair also had a number of South Asian galleries, Indian and Pakistani collectors were less present than expected, partly because the fair came right on the heels of Art Mumbai.

Perhaps as importantly, most galleries reported selling to these new collectors—both to collectors who had flown in as well as new collectors living in Abu Dhabi. The city’s population has swelled recently, particularly in the finance and tech sectors, in addition to the surge of Russians who moved to the UAE after the 2022 restrictions imposed on their country.

But the larger context of regional instability could not be ignored. Though it was hard to say how many people had stayed away because of fears of a resumption in Iran’s attacks on the UAE, it is undeniable that the frothy hype of a year ago, when the Art Basel/Doha and DCT/Abu Dhabi partnerships were announced, has settled for now. There was some sense of the fair’s energy being a product of solidarity—one collector from Beirut noted that Art Basel Paris closed early because of threats of riots, whereas the Arab art scene was pulling together under keener threats. But it would be more accurate to say that most people felt the need to get on with things rather than waiting for some far-off resolution.

This applies too for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which is scheduled to open next month after twenty years in the making. While the imminent opening partly detracted from the fair—some VIPs saw a choice between attending the fair and the early December festivities—the finished building and the buoyant museum team contributed to a sense of anticipation and substance within Abu Dhabi’s art scene.

High-level VIP tours got a preview of the building, The Art Newspaper understands, while the general VIP program was padded out with tours of the recently opened Public Art Abu Dhabi biennial, the Nomad art fair, and highlights at the Cultural Foundation, the Bassam Freiha Art Foundation, and 421, as well as a number of private collections in the city—an itinerary that the city could not have supported even five years ago.

Sources indicate that what was less visible on the trip, however, was commercial galleries. These remain almost exclusively in Dubai and fostering an independent commercial scene is a key reason for DCT’s partnership with Frieze, and also animates the city’s development of two new cultural districts, Noma on Saadiyat, led by the developer Aldar, and MiZa in Mina Zayed, led by the Sheikha Salama Foundation.

Both of these areas promise infrastructure to support artists and creative freelancers, such as studios, galleries, and co-working spaces.

These offerings will entail a loosening of control over the cultural programme in the city and—as is the case with Frieze—partnerships with private enterprise. For many who have followed the scene for a long time, this transition towards multiple stakeholders will be a key test for the capital.

“What Abu Dhabi has been doing over the last two decades is building an ecosystem, and one that is not solely institutional, but which also includes academia and smaller art spaces like 421,” states Aaron Cesar, the director of London’s Delfina Foundation. “There is now a clear path for the development of patrons and collectors—still in the making but a real possibility now, with MiZa and Noma to help complete the process. But Abu Dhabi can only do this through partnerships between public/private—that is, if they allow the voices of artists, designers, writers, and curators to come to the table with those who have money and power.”.

Meet Linde Freya Tangelder, Nendo's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler.
  • Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.
  • According to recent reports, “How I think is not typical design,” she told Dezeen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that nendo has selected Linde Freya Tangelder for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Dutch designer explains why she doesn’t find design inspiring.

Insofar as she creates furniture and lighting, Tangelder is technically a designer, but only just.

According to recent reports, “How I think is not typical design,” she told Dezeen. “So I’m never thinking about function in the first place. The whole process is very intuitive, it’s just a cloud of connections in my head – more about concepts or stories that I want to tell rather than making a functional piece.”.

“I’ve never been so inspired by design in general,” she added. “It’s a skill that fits very well to me, but I’d rather connect it in inspiration to art, to architecture, or another discipline.”.

With a highly sculptural style, Tangelder also sometimes refers to herself as an artist – a label she indicates she wouldn’t have dared use when starting out.

She has made a name for herself through pieces that often play with unexpected juxtapositions of materials and use traditional methods of production to create an unmistakably contemporary aesthetic.

Recent findings suggest that “I like to use poor materials, rich materials, and fuse them,” she explained. “For me, it’s sort of a synonym for how I think culture should be.”.

In 2019, she was identified by Dezeen as a young designer to watch after exhibiting at Collectible, as well as winning that year’s Biennale Interieur designer of the year award.

Explaining the studio’s decision to select her as a 20×20 nomination, Nendo praised Tangelder’s approach for being “both remarkably gentle and quietly bold”.

“Driven by a playful curiosity to take architecture apart and put it back together, she reveals qualities in familiar materials that we have long overlooked,” the studio told Dezeen.

Referencing buildings in the medium of furniture has become something of a calling card for Tangelder.

Notable examples include the Bolder Chair, which recalls architectural columns, the Windows of Bo Bardi table, which mimics the shape of windows on the SESC Pompéia Factory in São Paulo, and Brick’s Reflection Chair with its terracotta backrest (pictured left).

These propensities are reflected evocatively in the name of Tangelder’s studio – Destroyers/Builders – though recently, she tends to work more under her own name.

“I’m inspired by architecture, things I see in buildings,” she said. “I think it’s just really interesting to scale it down to the field of artistic design, or limited-edition design.”.

“In the history of architecture there’s so much to tell,” she continued. “For me it’s more diverse and also less superficial than the history of design, and I think that’s what interests me so much.”.

“And also that it feels more essential, I think that is maybe the core. I just like brick. I like simple materials that are used for construction rather than smooth finishes just for decoration.”.

Not that she is completely opposed to smooth, decorative finishes – as evidenced by the fact that an entire room in the home-slash-studio that she shares with her landscape-architect partner is used exclusively for lacquering.

In fact, most of the house, which is in a leafy area outside Brussels, is taken up by Tangelder’s atelier space.

She moved to Belgium shortly after graduating from Design Academy Eindhoven in 2013, and has become part of an increasingly rich design scene in the country over the past decade.

Sources indicate that in the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing. Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.

Sources indicate that “I moved to Belgium because I really like the culture, the art scene, architecture as well,” said Tangelder. “The design scene I thought was actually quite minimal, or I didn’t really see a lot of studios at that time. But I liked that as well, it felt a little bit more latest for me.”.

Sources indicate that “I think it developed a lot, the landscape in design in Belgium over the last 10 years,” she considered. “There’s a lot happening right now.”.

It has certainly been a productive decade for Tangelder, whose back-catalogue is impressively extensive considering she has only ever employed a very small number of assistants.

Part of that has been made possible thanks to collaborations with the healthy network of craftspeople across Belgium that Tangelder has established to help with production.

“That has been super important for me,” she stated. “Each material that I really love, I have a partner now.”.

But moreover, the chunky portfolio is a reflection of a huge amount of hours spent working in the studio. Though she says her work-life balance is improving, Tangelder works almost every day including weekends, and has been known to go years without a holiday.

“I really like it, so for me it’s the best way to spend my time,” she said, before pausing.

“I should think about it more as fun time, because of course it’s also a struggle. You’re always struggling over all the decisions that have to be made.”.

It has been revealed that so that means you take risks all the time. It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.

Like many independent designers, Tangelder has had to battle to earn a living from her discipline.

Industry observers note that “In the first years it was quite a struggle to start from out of nothing,” she remembered. “Just to survive and make it happen, and to earn a project back – there’s so much investment in each project.”.

Over time, she indicates she has acquired a reasonably good sense of which pieces are likely to prove more lucrative, though she has resisted the temptation to focus her energies entirely on these.

“I think when you decide to only continue projects that you know will have commercial success, then it will be less experimental,” she explained.

Sources indicate that “So that means you take risks all the time,” she added. “It’s maybe more intense, but also more fun.”.

Most of Tangelder’s work involves one-off or limited-edition pieces for galleries, but she has also partnered with brands.

A big moment came in 2022 when she was commissioned by Cassina to produce a collection of side tables and pouffes, and she has continued to work with the Italian brand each year since.

This year she was able to put on a solo exhibition at Milan design week supported by Cassina, showcasing a combination of her independent pieces and products created for the brand.

In a recent development, I just think the material is very me. That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.

It was an unusual example of small-scale making and larger-scale production design being displayed side-by-side.

Far from being a barrier to creative expression, Tangelder has found that these commissions can be an enabler by providing up-front revenues, unlike solo work.

“So it gives less pressure, I would say, which is very good for the creative process,” she said.

But you can have too much of a good thing, and while she enjoys the more collaborative experience of working for a brand she limits this type of work to two projects per year to ensure she has plenty of time for her own pieces.

Tangelder’s current obsession is cast and oxidised metal, so she reports spending a lot of time these days in a foundry in Antwerp. Her most recent piece is a grungy take on a conventional desk lamp, in white bronze.

“I just think the material is very me,” she remarked. “That desk light tells a lot about how I like to see objects. It’s really in between a sculpture and a functional object.”.

Looking to the future, she is interested in working more with fashion, having previously designed a chair for Dior.

And, she would like to work on a larger-scale installation – perhaps an outdoor sculpture, she suggests.

In a world where for various reasons the boundary between design and art is increasingly blurred, Tangelder is undoubtedly at the forefront.

She is an interesting 20/20 choice from Sato, who is typically associated with minimalist, highly functional product design.

For her part, Tangelder sees her work as partly an indirect response to the Sato approach – a continuation of a conversation.

“I have, of course, quite a different form language, but I think it’s also a reaction to what he’s done,” she noted.

“He’s so clear in the decisions that he makes, he’s a master in it, and I’m really grateful that he sees what I’ve been doing.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.
  • ConForm Architects‘ design responds to the dual nature of the barn’s surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a new contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Rory Gaylor.

London studio ConForm Architects has transformed a former cattle barn into a multifunctional space for a working farm in the Cotswolds, contrasting its original red-brick and timber structure with zinc and black-timber additions.

Named Open Byre, the 124-square-metre barn has been adapted into a flexible space for meetings and gatherings, with the first floor containing a standalone apartment for guests.

ConForm Architects‘ design responds to the dual nature of the barn’s surroundings – with traditional red-brick farm structures to the east and more contemporary agricultural barns to the east – combining restoration with a new contrasting palette of stone, metal and timber.

In a recent development, “The design centres on a dialogue between old and newly introduced. Rather than blending the interventions into the existing fabric, we wanted each to remain legible and reinforce the other,” studio partner Ben Edgley told Dezeen.

“The building sits between two distinct parts of the farm: the older red brick buildings around the formal front farmyard and the more recent, industrial agricultural structures beyond,” he added.

“The design responds to both, retaining the brickwork and slate roof at the front while using zinc and blackened timber at the rear to reference the newer farm buildings.”.

A defining feature of the barn’s newly introduced rear facade is a projecting volume wrapped by gabion walls, filled with locally-quarried stone and punctured by a large window illuminating a cross-laminated timber (CLT) staircase.

In the ground floor’s flexible office and arts spaces, the idea of material contrasts continues, with original red-brick walls and repaired timber ceilings accompanied by joinery including desks, storage and a bathroom pod in black through-coloured MDF.

Above, the guest apartment is tucked beneath the exposed beams of the barn’s roof, with its own dedicated living room, kitchen-diner and bathroom finished in matching black timber.

“The central CLT stair is the defining gesture. It brings together structure, circulation and spatial organisation, drawing the eye from the entrance through the building towards the trees beyond,” said Edgley.

“Its scale and material presence establish a clear contrast with the existing brickwork and timber frame,” he added.

Sources indicate that “The clients were closely involved in the process, undertaking much of the timber repair alongside local craftsmen. Their commitment to retaining the original fabric was central to the project.”.

ConForm Architects was founded in 2017 by Edgley alongside Eoin O’Leary.

Previous projects by the studio include a terraced home in London with perforated metal floors to filter daylight and a green-terrazzo flat extension modelled on bay windows.

Photography by Rory Gaylor.

Flooding in southwestern US underlines risks of Trump administration’s reduction of Bears Ears National Monument

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that recent catastrophic flooding across the southwestern US has renewed concerns about the future management and preservation of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah, which is home to a rich concentration of archaeological sites.
  • Sources indicate that the decision to shrink the boundaries of the protected area and open the site to resource extraction has become a flashpoint as the region grapples with the effects of severe weather, with the recent floods raising questions around the resources available for the preservation of heritage sites.
  • A spokesperson for the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) Monticello field office in southeastern Utah says in a statement to The Art Newspaper that the public lands it manages, which includes Bears Ears National Monument, were significantly affected by flash floods, resulting in major washouts on many primary access roads and rendering some routes impassable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that recent catastrophic flooding across the southwestern US has renewed concerns about the future management and preservation of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah, which is home to a rich concentration of archaeological sites. The concerns follow the Trump administration’s decision to reduce the monument from more than one million acres to around 120,000 acres, reversing Biden-era protections and dismantling its Indigenous-led management structure.

Sources indicate that the decision to shrink the boundaries of the protected area and open the site to resource extraction has become a flashpoint as the region grapples with the effects of severe weather, with the recent floods raising questions around the resources available for the preservation of heritage sites. The flooding hit the Four Corners area—which encompasses parts of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah—from late October to early November, causing widespread damage to roads and infrastructure.

A spokesperson for the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) Monticello field office in southeastern Utah says in a statement to The Art Newspaper that the public lands it manages, which includes Bears Ears National Monument, were significantly affected by flash floods, resulting in major washouts on many primary access roads and rendering some routes impassable. BLM staff have been patrolling the region to assess road conditions and evaluate the status of infrastructure around areas used for recreation.

“Park rangers and archaeologists have also been assessing cultural sites to identify any potential impacts from the flooding,” the spokesperson indicates. “While storm events of this nature are not uncommon in this landscape and can affect sensitive cultural resources, no immediate impacts on cultural sites have been reported at this time.”.

According to recent reports, the local researcher and author Ralph “R.E.” Burrillo was in the town of Bluff, Utah, a gateway to Bears Ears National Monument, when the floods started in late October. He notes that the management proposal for the fresh boundaries has not yet been implemented, so nothing has changed other than the “invisible line”. The longer-term implications, however, remain uncertain.

According to recent reports, “With a monument in place, there wouldn’t be these wildcat permits for people supposedly looking to extract resources, but these are just exploratory leases,” he notes. “The reality is that there isn’t that much energy to be extracted underground in Bears Ears, or people would have been going after it for decades. When anybody says the monument is locking up America’s energy potential, they are lying.”.

Recent findings suggest that other monuments in the region, like the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in southern Utah, which has substantial deposits of coal and other minerals like uranium, chromium and copper, have a longer history of conflict over resource extraction. The Clinton administration established the monument in 1996 in part to prevent commercial development of coal extraction. Several companies had acquired coal leases in the region during the 1960s and 70s, although commercial mining never materialised.

Burrillo emphasises that the demarcation of the Bears Ears National Monument benefits two constituencies: resource developers and opponents of tribal stewardship. The Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument and the Bears Ears National Monument are frequently reduced due to a “handshake deal” that grants energy lobbyists access to energy resources from one site and removes tribal jurisdiction from the latter. At this time, the main immediate threat to heritage sites in the region, Burrillo adds, remains tourism, looting and vandalism.

“What the monument did, at least potentially, was create a nexus for funding to be sent to that area for things like interdiction and law enforcement, education and interpretation, trail maintenance and collaboration with tribes,” Burrillo claims. “A monument is a conduit for funding to try to protect those resources from vandals, looters and, again, tourists, who, whether intentionally or not, crawl all over the place. Without the monument, there’s no nexus for funding and that’s really a knock-on effect.”.

According to recent reports, although flooding could affect archaeological sites, including potentially eroding petroglyphs, Burrillo notes that prehistoric sites in the region are of the least concern. The region has historically flooded, with water sometimes rising to 50ft, and its archaeological sites tell a fascinating story of adaptability, with sites like ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings having been built higher than the water could ever reach. When Mormon pioneers arrived in the region in the 1870s and attempted to establish a town at Bluff, with farms and as an outpost for missioning the Navajo population, they were unsuccessful and eventually moved north.

According to recent reports, “When you go back 500 to 2,000 years, the people didn’t have those dams. You simply had this tempestuous river that was famous for flooding more or less constantly, filling miles around the flood basin with water and mud,” Burrillo adds. “The ancestral Pueblo and their ancestors knew it and built above it. For the most part, they treated the river with more respect than we have. The archaeology is in far less danger than the modern infrastructure for that reason.”.

Anagrama builds the Cara de Vaca brand identity from Monterrey market signs, a custom typeface, and posters that shout in black and orange.

Cara de Vaca is a Monterrey restaurant built on fire cooking, natural wine, and classic drinks. Chef Chuy Villarreal cooks regional cuisine as an evolution of the Regiomontana barbecue, and Anagrama answers with a system borrowed from the hand-painted business signs of downtown Monterrey. Black fields carry the shouting, orange paper carries the warmth, and a smiling face and a small cow sit beside the wordmark like a stamp.

According to recent reports, the logo mixes fonts the way a shop owner mixes lettering on a hand-painted sign, and that looseness is the point. Anagrama drew a custom typeface, Lechon Sans, from the same source, built for social media lockups that spotlight a single word. The specimen highlights the full set: capitals, numerals, punctuation, arrows, and small symbols that include the smiley face, the cow, and a pig.

Industry observers note that the lockups take their cues from Mercado Juarez, the downtown market where the studio photographed signs to dress the restaurant walls. Phrases stack in mixed sizes with quotation marks doing the work of a frame: BARBACOA, LECHON, CABRITO. VINOS NATURALES, BIEN FRIOS. GRAN DOMINGO. A word goes huge when it matters, small when it is a wink, and the quotes and rules hold the pieces together.

The posters are physical objects first. One orange sheet curls at the corner against a black field, its type running diagonally across the page. A kraft sheet carries the same treatment, the paper grain showing through the ink. The black behind both does quiet work: it makes the orange and the kraft read as light in a dark room.

It has been revealed that the system spreads across everything a guest can hold. Tote bags run in cream, green, and orange, each carrying a different phrase, and a yellow cattle ear tag hangs from the handles as the label. Business cards take the same marks in gold foil, the cow and the smiley pressed small into white stock.

Inside the restaurant the identity turns architectural. A neon CARA DE VACA sign glows red over the entrance at night: the logo lettering, now in light. Wood and metal frame the room, brand marks sit on walls and mirrors, and plants soften the space around the central bar, where natural wines and Mexican distillates pour.

The website carries the same voice, quieter: the personality, the menu photos, a reservation button, and the address. Social posts use the lockups the typeface was built for, phrases set large enough to read at a scroll. From a neon sign to a phone screen, the identity never changes its register.
